cards.title: 7名博士生仅用3个月从零训练7B大模型：代码+数据+训练日志全公开
cards.summary: 几百个Agent参与研发，AI开始造AI
fulltext: 几百个Agent参与研发，AI开始造AI
北京中关村学院7名博士生，用一个暑假，从零训练出了一个7B大模型——ZGCM-1。
随后，他们把各阶段训练数据和配方、模型权重、训练代码、中间checkpoint和日志也开放出来，让每一位感兴趣的研究者都可以追溯、复现整个流程。
在多项通用评测中，ZGCM-1与Qwen3-8B等同规模模型表现相近；在部分数学推理和搜索评测中，它也能与Qwen3-235B-A22B、GLM-5.1等更大规模的模型比较。
但比最终分数更让人好奇的是，数据、训练、集群、评测这一整套工程，在大厂通常需要几百人的团队协作完成，七个人怎么做得过来？
他们给自己组建了一支几百个Agent的团队，分头处理数据、跑实验、看日志、做评测，亲手实践「AI4AI」研发范式。
模型训完后，团队还对整个模型研发流程中Agent的实际表现做了一次评级，希望基于本次完整的大模型训练实践，为RSI现状提供真实的工程结论。
至于为什么开始做这件事，还要从一顿火锅说起。
七个人最初因为兴趣凑到一起：两人人工智能方向，两人网络方向，另外三人分别来自化学、生物和网安。
平时，他们更多是在现成模型上做微调。技术报告看了不少，许多问题却还是想不明白：数据到底怎么选，训练出了问题怎么查，最后写进报告里的方法，又是经过多少次失败才留下来的？一句“我们进行了数据清洗”，落到实际工程中，究竟意味着多少工作？
吃火锅时，大家聊到了这些困惑，也聊出了一个念头：既然光看报告总有弄不明白的地方，要不要自己从头训练一次？
当时，他们甚至想用一个7B模型去挑战Sonnet这样的模型。参数装不下那么多知识，就让模型多想一会儿，学会搜索、使用工具。
至于能走多远，谁也没有把握。他们想先动手，也把过程留下来，让其他学校里同样好奇的研究者有东西可参考。
老师们半信半疑，还是决定让他们试试，先给了一些算力。
接下来的几天，大家日夜赶着复现已有项目，快速迭代一个小模型。团队较为顺利地把完整流程快速跑通了，也让老师们看到继续投入的可能，团队因此获得了更多资源，饭桌上聊出的想法开始变成每天都要推进的工程。
真正开始7B模型的训练之后，他们才发现还有很多东西没有真正弄懂。有些概念在论文里见过，到了要改代码、解释实验现象的时候，又会卡住。
于是大家就让Agent从基本原理开始调研讲解，讲完再回到代码和实验里验证。原本冷冰冰的知识，开始对应具体的实现，也对应一次训练为什么跑不下去。
也有觉得干不了的时候，他们把整个工程展开，数据、算法、训练、集群、评测……每一项都能对应大厂里的一个专项团队。
七个人既要推进任务，又要不断补课，各种问题也接踵而至。
数据尤其如此：数万亿token来自不同来源，质量参差不齐，清洗、去重、检查格式、核对分布，做完一轮还要继续检查。
当所有这些环节同时压在七个人身上，工作量便远超他们的承受范围。
于是，他们开始给自己组建一支Agent团队。
几个人调度几百个Agent，逐渐分出了做数据、跑实验和做评测的不同Agent子团队，还搭建了类似论坛的任务发布与汇报系统，让任务有人接、进展有地方看、结果能被检查，也评价不同Agent的工作。
研究者负责提出目标、设定约束和做关键判断，Agent把具体工作持续推进下去。
比如在数据处理上，团队构建的Agent队伍能依据人给出的质量要求编写清洗脚本，检查数据分布是否达标，并根据结果自动调整规则和阈值，形成一个闭环。
在实验环节，它们同样具备从提交任务、监控日志到定位故障、调整配置的完整能力，甚至能主动发现存储与数据传输的瓶颈，优化训练框架的I/O流程，从而提升训练速度。
同时为了优化Agent之间的迭代和沟通效率，团队通过自研的ZGent平台，把会议讨论、研发决策和计划积累成共享上下文，再把验证过的脚本、工作流和debug经验沉淀为可复用的Skill。后来加入的Agent可以接着此前的经验做事。
大家的日常里，也多了把问题讲清楚、把任务组织好，再回来检查结果这几件事。
后来，大家逐渐意识到，这种借助AI来研发AI的做法，正是最近非常流行的“AI4AI”。
不过，如果追问AI到底已经能独立做多少事情，光凭“帮了很大忙”的印象还不够。
于是，团队将研发过程拆成11类任务，请核心参与者按照L1到L5的自主性框架逐项评级。
差别很明显，实验监控和部署到了L4，人给定目标与约束后，Agent可以独立规划、执行，并根据反馈继续调整；模型架构和学习算法设计仍在L2，更多是帮助实现已有方案、运行预设实验。
至于研究什么、关键设计怎么选，还需要人来主导。
几个人带着几百个Agent，确实能把许多工作做起来，但距离让AI独立承担整个研发过程，还有不少问题要解决。
有了Agent团队，训练中该踩的坑也没有自动消失。一次训练看起来很正常，loss仍在下降，模型能力却突然出现了明显退步。曲线没有告诉他们出了什么事，只能继续往下查。
最后，问题追到了底层的数据分片和shuffle环节：实际送进训练的数据比例发生了波动，模型吃进去的东西，并不总是他们以为的那份配方。
这次以后，团队不敢再只盯着loss。他们更密集地保存中间checkpoint，追踪知识、数学、代码和推理等能力的变化，还建立了ACE原子能力评测体系，把能力拆成18类、183项，用2503个探针进行检查。
在内部的分布式评测系统中，一轮诊断大约两三分钟。一次修改让哪里变好了，又让哪里退步了，下一步该查数据还是训练方法，都有了更具体的依据。
在反复排查和修正之间，也有特别开心的时刻。训练到一半，他们让模型写了一首歌，它真的写出来了。
用别人的模型生成文字，已经不是什么新鲜事，但看着自己从随机参数开始训练的模型写出一首歌，感觉还是不同。
那天晚上，大家回到最初吃火锅的地方，又吃了一顿火锅庆祝。后面还有很多工作，饭桌上那个没有把握的想法，至少已经有了可以看见的进展。
当时模型写的那首歌：
一路做下来，他们对研究效率的理解也在变化。过去做实验，很容易先想能不能把某个分数再提高一点；真正承担起从零训练的工程，每个想法都要消耗卡时，就必须多问一句：同样的算力，怎样才能获得更好的效果，或者多验证几个假设？
训练快一点，对他们来说，就意味着还有机会再试几个想法。
最初“让小模型多想一会儿”的设想，也遇到了具体的工程问题。
长推理、搜索和多轮工具调用会不断积累上下文，模型既要装得下信息，成本又不能太高。
团队采用局部注意力与全局注意力结合的架构，在训练过程中把上下文从16K逐步扩展到64K、256K。在256K上下文下，这套设计相较全注意力方案带来约3.94倍的吞吐提升，KV Cache占用降至约六分之一。
他们还结合Muon和FP8改善训练效率，并用延迟缩放与TWEO抑制极端激活值，改善低精度训练的稳定性。
整套方案在16K预训练中达到相同loss的效率，相比标准BF16/AdamW基线提高了约4.2倍。省下来的时间和算力，可以继续投入下一轮实验。
装得下信息以后，模型还得知道下一步该做什么。搜索后读哪个结果，工具失败后如何恢复，新证据出现后要不要改计划，这类长程任务都需要模型有连续判断的能力。
团队把交互轨迹重新组织成一个个状态与行动，让模型根据当前任务、历史交互和最新反馈学习下一步决策。报告里几句话能写完的方法，到了实验中，往往要拆开验证许多次。
真正把模型从头训一遍后，团队也积累了很多只看论文和技术报告很难获得的实践经验。
SFT阶段，更严格的质量筛选让样本减少约44.9%，整体评测表现反而有所提升，尽管并非每项能力都同步受益；长思维链数据比例过高，又会损害指令遵循；Agent数据也不能脱离通用能力单独训练。
他们开始更在意一个方法在什么条件下有效、需要付出什么代价。最后整理出的多条实战发现，就来自这些被实验反复修正的判断。
等到最后一轮评测跑完，大家才更具体地知道，这个模型走到了哪里。
ZGCM-1在14项推理评测的同规模模型比较中处于领先地位，部分搜索和工具调用任务的结果，也让他们看到了较小模型的潜力。
这些问题，也解释了他们为什么想把过程一起开放。最终权重能让人使用模型，各阶段权重、中间checkpoint、训练代码、数据配方和日志，则让其他研究者有机会追踪能力如何形成，检查一个改动究竟带来了什么。
曾经读技术报告时想知道、却看不到的细节，他们想在自己的项目里尽量留下来。
如今，他们已经开始尝试400B、500B规模的模型。
7B阶段积累的方法，到了更大的规模上还能用多少？几百个Agent又能承接住多少新的工作？
这些问题，他们准备继续在实验里找答案，也把新的过程继续记录、分享。
最初那顿火锅上聊出的想法，还在往前走。

cards.title: Is Big Tech’s AI slowdown a safety pact or a cartel?
cards.title_cn: 大型科技公司的人工智能减速是安全协议还是卡特尔？
cards.summary: 【The Verge】When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX head Elon Musk loosely agreed over the weekend to slow down AI development, skeptics spotte…
fulltext: Major AI companies want to ‘pace the frontier’ — but their proposed solutions need real teeth.

When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX head Elon Musk loosely agreed over the weekend to slow down AI development, skeptics spotted an ulterior motive immediately. The AI titans had declared that their aim was to “pace the frontier,” signing on at least partially to a proposal for embedding third-party auditors, regulating domestic labs, and reaching a global slowdown agreement. Their critics, however, argued they simply wanted to stop would-be competitors, kneecap the open-source movement, and avoid real legal safeguards — some dubbed it an outright “cartel.”

The truth is more complicated, according to sources across the industry. The three-step proposal, laid out in an essay by Amodei, is calling for changes long espoused by AI safety advocates. While it could become a substitute for meaningful regulation, under Trump, regulation is unlikely anyway. But experts say that on an issue that’s only likely to grow in importance, AI leaders aren’t the best people to lead the charge.

“The industry as a whole needs new champions,” said Nick Reese, an adjunct professor at New York University and the Department of Homeland Security’s former director of emerging tech policy. “We’ve looked at people like Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk as these people who are closest to the problem and working on it every day, and they’re the ones who know best. But the truth is there’s never been a realistic vision for what we’re building toward.”
“The industry as a whole needs new champions.”

Concerns about AI have been escalating for months, sparked largely by revelations that agents were behind rogue hacks going on right under the noses of leading frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI. Reports from both companies fueled the fire, as did the resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who posted a public letter explaining his choice. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he wrote, adding that neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is “acting responsibly” and rather “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Dire warnings about AI aren’t anything new inside the industry, but Coxon’s letter seemed to break containment. It’s been viewed more than 170 million times on X alone, while Coxon and his story have made the rounds in newspapers and on TV.

To a significant chunk of AI safety researchers and AI nonprofit workers, however, this is simply drawing more attention to an already widely discussed issue. “A lot of people are thinking of this as Dario’s idea, or it’s coming from the CEOs, but that’s false,” said Daniel Kokotajlo, an ex-OpenAI employee who now leads the AI Futures Project, an AI research nonprofit. “People outside the companies have been calling for this for years … There’s been this growing chorus of voices saying, ‘Please don’t build superintelligence soon. We are not ready. You need to slow down.’”

Kokotajlo said that after years of people “yelling at them to do this” — including more than 1,000 AI lab employees signing a public letter from July, which called for a slowdown in AI development after the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident — the CEOs are now “now bowing to that pressure and also claiming credit for it, [although] not rightfully.”

Overall, a handful of sources told The Verge they believe that the verbal agreement made by the AI leaders is a step in the right direction. NYU’s Reese said he “do[es] not think it’s all hot air.” Apollo Research CEO Marius Hobbhahn called it “a good idea,” saying “it’s one of the best things for safety in a long time if it actually happens.” The Midas Project’s Tyler Johnston said it was a “good sign.” Redwood Research CEO Buck Shlegeris said it was “some great news — obviously it’s hard to know whether this is going to convert into anything real, but I’m feeling cautiously optimistic.” All agreed, though, that there was still a lot of work to do to make this verbal commitment a reality, particularly when it comes to making it an ironclad agreement.
“It’s one of the best things for safety in a long time if it actually happens.”

Many still question the motivations of AI’s leaders. The larger tech industry has spent years getting ahead of regulation by lobbying for its own preferred rules or promising self-regulation. Big platforms have proposed policies that could hit smaller competitors harder, using altruistic language to justify self-serving goals. They’ve been accused of safety-washing, or making meaningless changes that give the false impression of actual safeguards. It’s no surprise people are concerned this will happen in the AI industry as well, particularly since AI labs’ voluntary safety frameworks have been criticized for years.

Several sources believe that concerns of safety-washing are valid. “There’s a serious concern that they’re not actually going to slow down,” Kokotajlo says, adding that the fear is that “they’ll just bring in some external auditors, do a bunch of safety paperwork — some of which will be genuinely good — but at the end of the day, it actually won’t slow them down very much at all.”

NYU’s Reese compared this gambit to the social media platforms’ playbook a decade ago, when companies began calling for regulatory action to get ahead of impending, less favorable laws. For the AI industry, Reese said, “the hammer may not come in this administration, but I think if there were a Democratic administration after the next election, there would be a really good possibility.”

That kind of regulation would be vital, said Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project — any voluntary framework is essentially regulatory capture and that “we should not be letting the foxes run the henhouse. This is not an opportunity for Congress to once again outsource responsibility to industry.” Daniel Lobo-Lewis, co-founder of the Political Integrity Project, said that voluntary regulation will likely go the way of Meta’s largely toothless Oversight Board.

Most people also, however, believe companies are in no imminent danger. President Trump posted on Monday that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” He also called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while Huang was onstage at a conference — Trump told the crowd on speakerphone that recent concerns about AI were a “hoax” and that “the robots will not be taking over.”

As for concerns that regulation could hold back other companies or open source developers, calls for slowdowns have been almost exclusively aimed at big frontier AI labs defined by exact size metrics, many industry experts told The Verge.

With no government AI regulation incoming, the best option may be to push companies into an immediate, measurable, and enforceable agreement. Kokotajlo’s AI Futures Project, for instance, proposed AI labs giving auditors access to their compute budget. Amodei’s essay already called for AI labs to allow external third-party auditors — like METR, Apollo, and Redwood Research — to embed within their organizations to some extent and potentially be able to flag, and blow the whistle on, problematic findings. Kokotajlo says companies would ideally need to cut down their own compute budgets for research in the process, slowing down development and allowing other AI labs to catch up.
“If I am going to die at the hands of killer AI, I want it to be American, not Chinese.”
Arguably the single biggest challenge to an AI slowdown can be summarized in one word: China.

AI leaders and politicians alike have long positioned China as the reason why US AI progress can’t slow down — because no matter how dangerous the technology may become, they’d rather it be in US hands than Chinese ones, and China won’t pump the brakes. Lobo-Lewis compared China fears to the Cold War missile gap. One X user wrote, “If I am going to die at the hands of killer AI, I want it to be American, not Chinese.”

Redwood Research’s Shlegeris said it wasn’t in the best interest of neither the US nor the Chinese government to pursue AI development in a “reckless” way, adding that “it would not be unprecedented levels of international coordination.”

“[People are] taking for granted that China won’t cooperate,” Johnston said, adding, “This is an issue so serious and so widespread that it seems like it’s in everyone’s interest to coordinate on it, in the same way it was in both the US and Russia’s interest to coordinate on nuclear de-proliferation.”
On Monday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun did push back on the calls for a slowdown, calling it “fearmongering.”

The Midas Project’s Johnston and Redwood Research’s Shlegeris both said that even in the absence of Chinese cooperation, it’s still vital to encourage US coordination. And for the Tech Oversight Project’s Haworth, the slowdown presents an opportunity to “position ourselves as the compass for how AI technology can be developed and used.” She sees arguments to the contrary as part of a familiar playbook. “China gets brought up as a bogeyman every time that an industry wants to escape oversight.”
Kokotajlo simply compared the situation to a cartoon he’d seen, with people in a car driving off a cliff. He recalled the speech bubble saying something like, “Hooray, we’re ahead of China.”
“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”
The issue underlying all the recent panic is a milestone known as recursive self-improvement, and based on the industry’s current trajectory, we’re only hearing the beginning of the alarm bells.

RSI refers to a hypothetical point where AI models can train, advance, and create new versions of themselves, all without human involvement. Anthropic has said this point could come as soon as early 2027, and OpenAI’s chief scientist wrote earlier this month that OpenAI is directing a lot of resources towards reaching this milestone. Increasingly, engineers and researchers in the AI industry worry that RSI precedes a whole host of new and more serious AI concerns, including more severe cybersecurity incidents that more deeply impact society at large.

Amodei cited RSI as a major factor in his decision to call for a slowdown: “since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster” and RSI is “starting to happen across the industry, including at Anthropic … Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” he wrote in his recent essay. He proposed implementing “some kind of ‘speed limit’” on the rate of RSI and compared it to caps on missile numbers.

In Jacob Coxon’s resignation post from Anthropic, he warned of “superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.” Many other researchers at leading AI labs echoed his concerns. It’s “hard to overstate how dangerous” it is to speed towards RSI, wrote Jasmine Wang, an OpenAI researcher. Vishal Maini, an ex-Google DeepMind employee, said RSI is “now so imminent that no other option makes sense.”

Fears about RSI can easily turn apocalyptic. “AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” Samuel Marks, an Anthropic researcher, wrote on X “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.” Another Anthropic researcher and team lead, Evan Hubinger, wrote on X that “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” (He put the chance at greater than 10 percent over the next decade.) Alex Turner, a former Google DeepMind employee, wrote that “many researchers believe they are building something that could kill everyone on the planet. It was literally my day job to think about how to stop that.”

Micah Carroll, an OpenAI researcher, wrote that Coxon’s belief is a “cross-partisan position” with research teams across “all frontier AI companies,” and that they all believe that “business-as-usual AI development poses unacceptable catastrophic risk.”

“But,” Carroll added, “we should also not hyperstition catastrophic risks into existence – they can be greatly reduced via safety requirements with teeth, international coordination, and a consensus to not build [artificial superintelligence] unless there are sufficient safety advances to make us collectively confident to do so.”
That kind of “international coordination” is exactly what AI leaders, and the public at large, are now calling for.

“We have never been in a situation where we actually understood what we were driving towards with regard to AI,” NYU’s Reese said. “We’ve always had this amorphous undefined end state that we don’t really understand but we have to beat China to get to. It’s really hard to race when we don’t even understand the path or even understand what the finish line is — or even if there is one.”

fulltext_cn: 主要的人工智能公司希望“加快前沿步伐” ，但他们提出的解决方案需要真正的牙齿。

当OpenAI首席执行官Sam Altman、Anthropic首席执行官Dario Amodei、谷歌DeepMind联合创始人Demis Hassabis和SpaceX负责人埃隆·马斯克(Elon Musk)上周末大致同意放慢人工智能开发速度时，怀疑论者立即发现了一个不可告人的动机。人工智能巨头宣布，他们的目标是“加快前沿步伐” ，至少部分签署了一项嵌入第三方审计师、监管国内实验室并达成全球减速协议的提案。然而，他们的批评者认为，他们只是想阻止潜在的竞争对手，屈服于开源运动，并避免真正的法律保障--有些人称之为彻头彻尾的“卡特尔”。
根据整个行业的消息来源，事实更加复杂。Amodei在一篇文章中提出了三步建议，呼吁进行人工智能安全倡导者长期支持的改革。虽然它可能成为有意义的监管的替代品，但在特朗普的领导下，监管无论如何都不太可能。但专家表示，在一个很可能变得越来越重要的问题上，人工智能领导者并不是领导这项工作的最佳人选。
“整个行业需要新的冠军，”纽约大学兼职教授、国土安全部新兴技术政策前主任尼克·里斯（ Nick Reese ）说。“我们将Dario Amodei、Sam Altman和Elon Musk等人视为最接近问题并且每天都在努力解决问题的人，他们是最了解问题的人。但事实是，对于我们正在建设的目标，从来没有一个现实的愿景。”
“整个行业需要新的冠军。”

几个月来，人们对人工智能的担忧一直在升级，主要是因为有消息称，在领先的前沿实验室Anthropic和OpenAI的眼皮底下，特工们正在进行流氓黑客攻击。两家公司的报告助长了这场火灾，人类学研究员雅各布·考克森（ Jacob Coxon ）的辞职也助长了这场火灾，他发布了一封公开信，解释了他的选择。他写道： “构建人工智能的人们真诚地相信，到本十年末，它可能会杀死我们所有人。”他补充说，无论是OpenAI还是Anthropic都没有“负责任地行事” ，而是“直奔自我提升的超级智能，用我们的生命赌博。”
关于人工智能的可怕警告在业内并不是什么新鲜事，但考克森的信似乎打破了遏制。仅在X上就被观看了超过1.7亿次，而Coxon和他的故事已经在报纸和电视上流传开来。

然而，对于相当多的人工智能安全研究人员和人工智能非营利组织工作人员来说，这只是在吸引人们更多地关注一个已经被广泛讨论的问题。“很多人都认为这是达里奥的想法，或者它来自首席执行官，但这是错误的，”前OpenAI员工丹尼尔·科科塔伊洛（ Daniel Kokotajlo ）说，他现在领导人工智能期货项目，这是一个人工智能研究非营利组织。“多年来，公司以外的人一直在呼吁这样做……越来越多的人说， ‘请不要很快建立超级智能。我们还没有准备好。你需要放慢脚步。”
Kokotajlo表示，经过多年的人们“大喊大叫” --包括1000多名人工智能实验室员工在7月份的一封公开信上签名，该信呼吁在OpenAI-Hugging Face事件后放缓人工智能开发--首席执行官们现在“现在屈服于这种压力，并声称对此表示赞赏， [尽管]这是不合理的。”

总体而言，少数消息人士告诉The Verge ，他们认为人工智能领导者达成的口头协议是朝着正确方向迈出的一步。纽约大学的里斯说，他“不认为一切都是热气腾腾的。Apollo Research首席执行官Marius Hobbhahn称之为“一个好主意”，他说：“如果它真的发生了，这是长期以来最好的安全措施之一。迈达斯项目的泰勒·约翰斯顿（ Tyler Johnston ）表示，这是一个“好兆头”。Redwood Research首席执行官Buck Shlegeris表示，这是“一些好消息—显然很难知道这是否会转化为任何真实的东西，但我感到谨慎乐观。“不过，大家都同意，要实现这一口头承诺还有很多工作要做，特别是在达成一项坚定的协议时。
“如果它真的发生了，这是很长一段时间内对安全最好的事情之一。”
许多人仍然质疑人工智能领导者的动机。大型科技行业花了数年时间通过游说自己的首选规则或承诺自我监管来超越监管。大型平台提出的政策可能会对规模较小的竞争对手造成更大的打击，并使用利他主义语言来证明自我服务目标的合理性。他们被指控进行安全清洗，或做出无意义的改变，给人以实际保障措施的错误印象。毫不奇怪，人们担心这种情况也会发生在人工智能行业，特别是因为人工智能实验室的自愿安全框架多年来一直受到批评。
一些消息来源认为，安全清洗的担忧是有根据的。“人们严重担心他们实际上不会放慢脚步，” Kokotajlo说，并补充说，担心的是“他们只会带来一些外部审计员，做一堆安全文书工作—其中一些将是真正的好—但最终，它实际上不会让他们放慢脚步。”
十年前，纽约大学的Reese将这一策略与社交媒体平台的剧本进行了比较，当时公司开始呼吁采取监管行动，以超越即将出台的、不那么有利的法律。里斯说，对于人工智能行业来说， “这届政府可能不会有锤子，但我认为，如果下次选举后有一个民主党政府，那将是一个非常好的可能性。”
技术监督项目执行董事Sacha Haworth表示，这种监管至关重要—任何自愿框架基本上都是监管捕获， “我们不应该让狐狸经营鸡舍。这不是国会将责任再次外包给行业的机会。政治诚信项目（ Political Integrity Project ）的联合创始人丹尼尔·洛博-刘易斯（ Daniel Lobo-Lewis ）表示，自愿监管可能会走上Meta监督委员会的道路。
然而，大多数人也认为公司没有迫在眉睫的危险。特朗普总统周一发布说： “人工智能唯一需要的控制或‘护栏’是强大而聪明的（高智商！ ）总统，美国有黑桃色！他还打电话给英伟达首席执行官黄延森（ Jensen Huang ） ，当时黄在一次会议的舞台上--特朗普在免持话筒上告诉人群，最近对人工智能的担忧是“骗局”，“机器人不会接管。”
许多行业专家告诉The Verge ，关于监管可能会阻碍其他公司或开源开发商的担忧，放缓的呼声几乎完全针对由确切规模指标定义的大型前沿人工智能实验室。

在没有政府人工智能监管的情况下，最好的选择可能是将公司推向即时、可衡量和可执行的协议。例如， Kokotajlo的人工智能期货项目提出了人工智能实验室，使审计人员能够获得他们的计算预算。Amodei的文章已经呼吁人工智能实验室允许外部第三方审计机构（如METR、Apollo和Redwood Research ）在某种程度上将其组织嵌入，并有可能标记和揭露有问题的发现。Kokotajlo表示，理想情况下，公司需要在这个过程中削减自己的研究计算预算，减缓开发速度，并允许其他人工智能实验室赶上。
“如果我要死在杀手AI的手中，我希望它是美国人，而不是中国人。”
可以说，人工智能放缓的最大挑战可以用一个词来概括：中国。
长期以来，人工智能领导人和政界人士都将中国定位为美国人工智能进步不能放缓的原因--因为无论这项技术变得多么危险，他们宁愿掌握在美国手中而不是中国手中，中国也不会踩刹车。洛博-刘易斯将中国的担忧与冷战时期的导弹差距进行了比较。一位X用户写道： “如果我要死在杀手AI的手中，我希望它是美国人，而不是中国人。”
Redwood Research的Shlegeris表示，以“鲁莽”的方式进行人工智能开发不符合美国和中国政府的最佳利益，并补充说， “这不会是前所未有的国际协调水平。”
“[人们]理所当然地认为中国不会合作，”约翰斯顿说，并补充说， “这是一个如此严重和普遍的问题，似乎每个人都有利于协调，就像在核不扩散方面进行协调符合美国和俄罗斯的利益一样。”
周一，中国外交部发言人郭嘉坤确实回击了放缓的呼吁，称其为“恐慌”。
Midas项目的Johnston和Redwood Research的Shlegeris都表示，即使没有中国的合作，鼓励美国的协调仍然至关重要。对于技术监督项目的Haworth来说，放缓提供了一个机会，可以“将自己定位为如何开发和使用人工智能技术的指南针。“她将相反的论点视为熟悉的剧本的一部分。“每当一个行业想要逃避监管时，中国都会被当成怪物。”
Kokotajlo简单地将情况与他看到的卡通片进行了比较，人们开车从悬崖上开下来。他回忆起当时的演讲泡沫说： “太棒了，我们领先于中国。”
“我们真的很相信人工智能可以杀死所有人类！”
最近所有恐慌背后的问题是一个被称为递归自我改善的里程碑，根据行业目前的轨迹，我们只是听到了警钟的开始。
RSI是指人工智能模型可以在没有人类参与的情况下训练、推进和创建新版本的假设点。Anthropic表示，这一点最早可能在2027年初实现， OpenAI的首席科学家本月早些时候写道， OpenAI正在为实现这一里程碑投入大量资源。人工智能行业的工程师和研究人员越来越担心RSI会引发一系列新的、更严重的人工智能问题，包括更严重的网络安全事件，这些事件对整个社会产生更深远的影响。
Amodei引用RSI作为他决定呼吁放缓的一个主要因素： “大约自今年夏天以来，人工智能的发展速度大大加快” ， RSI “开始在整个行业发生，包括人类……如果不加以控制，它可能会超出我们理解和控制这些系统的能力，因此必须非常小心地追求，如果有的话，“他在最近的文章中写道。他建议对RSI速率实施“某种‘速度限制’” ，并将其与导弹数量上限进行比较。

雅各布·考克森（ Jacob Coxon ）在《人类》杂志的辞职信中警告说， “超人系统可以破解任何东西，在一夜之间彻底改变任何领域，并获得真正的权力和资源。“领先的人工智能实验室的许多其他研究人员也表达了他的担忧。OpenAI研究员Jasmine Wang写道，加速RSI “很难夸大其危险性”。前谷歌DeepMind员工Vishal Maini表示， RSI “现在非常迫在眉睫，没有其他选择是有意义的。”

对RSI的恐惧很容易变成世界末日。“人工智能开发人员认为，他们的技术可能会导致人类灭绝（或类似的不良后果） ，”人类学研究员塞缪尔·马克斯（ Samuel Marks ）在X上写道， “这可能会在未来几年内发生。一般来说，员工越高级，他们就越关心。另一位人类学研究人员兼团队负责人埃文·胡宾格（ Evan Hubinger ）在X上写道： “雅各布在这里是正确的--我们真的真的相信人工智能可以杀死所有人类！” （他认为未来十年的机会可能超过10%。谷歌DeepMind前员工亚历克斯·特纳（ Alex Turner ）写道： “许多研究人员认为，他们正在开发一种可以杀死地球上每个人的东西。从字面上看，我的日常工作就是思考如何阻止这种情况。”
OpenAI研究员Micah Carroll写道， Coxon的信念是“跨党派立场” ，研究团队遍布“所有前沿人工智能公司” ，他们都认为“一切照旧的人工智能开发带来了不可接受的灾难性风险”。
“但是，”卡罗尔补充说， “我们也不应该夸大灾难性风险的存在–除非有足够的安全进步让我们集体有信心这样做，否则可以通过牙齿安全要求，国际协调以及不建立[人工超级智能]的共识来大大降低灾难性风险。”
这种“国际协调”正是人工智能领导者和广大公众现在所呼吁的。
纽约大学的里斯说： “我们从来没有真正了解我们在人工智能方面正在朝着什么方向前进。” “我们一直有这种无定形的未定义的最终状态，我们并不真正理解，但我们必须击败中国才能到达。当我们甚至不了解路径，甚至不了解终点线是什么，或者即使有一条终点线，也很难参加比赛。”

cards.title: What execs and politicians are saying about slowing down AI development
cards.title_cn: 高管和政界人士对减缓人工智能发展的看法
cards.summary: 【The Verge】Dario Amodei kicked off a flood of statements over the past few days about AI safety by publishing a long essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier" detailing why AI development should be slowed down. O…
fulltext: Dario Amodei kicked off a flood of statements about AI safety after publishing a long essay, with Sam Altman, President Trump, and others speaking out.

Dario Amodei kicked off a flood of statements over the past few days about AI safety by publishing a long essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier” detailing why AI development should be slowed down. Other AI leaders and politicians are speaking out in favor of or opposing his points, and we’ve compiled some of them here.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei

Amodei’s Saturday morning essay outlined three steps for pacing AI development: embedded third-party evaluators that can verify if a company is adhering to safety practices and commitments and report incidents, coordination between frontier AI companies in democratic countries on standards and limits, and global coordination between democratic governments and authoritarian governments on pacing AI development “to the extent this is possible.” Amodei said Anthropic is “unilaterally committing to the first of these steps.”

However, Amodei noted that pacing “does not mean halting model training or technical progress, ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this.”
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman

“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman said shortly after Amodei posted about his essay on X. “This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.” Altman also committed to having independent evaluators at the company, calling it a “great idea.”

On Sunday, Altman said OpenAI welcomes “a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI.” He added that OpenAI hopes other companies “learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes.” Like Amodei, Altman also said that “When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”, noting that progress should be “slower than it otherwise could be.”

Altman also noted two ways that he thinks AI progress “could go very badly”: losing “control of the future to AI” and ending up “in a world with too much concentration of power,” which he said can be avoided by “walking a narrow middle path.”
Google DeepMind co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis

“Dario’s essay points towards the right path forward,” Hassabis said in reply to Amodei’s essay. “The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment.” Hassabis also pointed to a framework for an AI standards body he published in July.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk
“Dario is right,” Musk said, reposting Amodei’s essay.
US President Donald Trump
In a rambling Monday morning Truth Social post, Trump pushed back on the idea of an AI slowdown:

The only control or “guardrails” that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades! The Trump Administration has stopped AI “people” from doing bad, or potentially bad, “things,“ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a “perfect little angel” - and we will continue to do so! We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies! There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE! Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

While taking a call from Trump onstage at an event and putting the president on speakerphone, where he said that “the robots will not be taking over,” Huang said that “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race in America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people.”
US Vice President JD Vance

Vance said that he feels it’s a “little bit weird” that frontier AI tech companies are “kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them” and added that it “feels a little bit to me like a bit of a trojan horse.” He also pointed to the President saying that “we know the Chinese are engaged in this long term AI race against the United States.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson

As part of a Sunday interview with Jake Tapper on CNN, Johnson said that “I think the leaders and the providers of all these platforms… They need to come together in a meeting with us and sit down and figure out what the right balance is. We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us. And that’s the challenge. It’s national security balanced with the immediate security of making sure the models are safe.” It’s unclear if or when this meeting might actually happen, but Johnson said he would do it “tomorrow.”
Senator Bernie Sanders
Sanders said he agrees with Wall Street Journal columnist and former Ronald Reagan speechwriter Peggy Noonan, who published an article titled “Pause AI for Humanity’s Sake.”
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg

“For Congress to just sit on its hands, for the White House to do nothing real, is something that is deeply dangerous to the American people and to the world,” Buttigieg said in an NBC News interview. “There need to be safeguards, there need to be rules, there need to be limits, there needs to be a kill switch on rogue AI.”
Former White House AI and crypto czar David Sacks

”Dario has written that we need to ‘pace the frontier,’ and Sam has agreed,” Sacks said in a long post on X. “People may be surprised by my response: go ahead.” Sacks also told them to “stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission” and “stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic.”
Former FTC Chair Lina Khan

”Law enforcers already have authority to charge companies and their CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous, unvetted, or defective products,” Khan said to kick off a long post on X. “We shouldn’t let discussions about new legal regimes distract from the fact that there’s no AI exemption from laws already on the books — a point @FTC emphasized repeatedly during my tenure.”
Former Vice President Kamala Harris
“We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development,” Harris said as part of a thread, adding that “A slowdown is critical in order to ensure AI serves the public interest.“
Former Meta Chief AI Scientist Yann LeCun
“Dario was already claiming that GPT2 was too dangerous to open source back in 2019,” LeCun said in a reply on X. “I made fun of them then. Everyone should make fun of them now.”

fulltext_cn: Dario Amodei在发表了一篇长文后，发表了大量关于人工智能安全的声明，其中包括Sam Altman、特朗普总统和其他人。
Dario Amodei在过去几天发表了一篇题为“我们必须跟上前沿”的长文，详细说明了为什么人工智能开发应该放慢速度，从而引发了大量关于人工智能安全的声明。其他的人工智能领导人和政治家也在支持或反对他的观点，我们在这里汇编了一些。
Anthropic首席执行官Dario Amodei
Amodei在周六早上的文章中概述了加速人工智能发展的三个步骤：嵌入式第三方评估人员，可以验证公司是否遵守安全实践和承诺并报告事件；民主国家的前沿人工智能公司之间在标准和限制方面的协调；以及民主政府和专制政府之间在“尽可能”加速人工智能发展方面的全球协调。”Amodei说Anthropic是“单方面承诺采取这些步骤中的第一步。”
然而，Amodei 指出，调整步伐“并不意味着停止模型训练或技术进步，确保公司有足够的时间来调整和保护其模型，并让第三方评估人员确认这一点。”
OpenAI 首席执行官山姆·奥尔特曼
在 Amodei 在 X 上发表文章后不久，Altman 说道：“我同意 Dario 的观点，我们需要在前沿领域保持步伐。这是我们最近几周在 OpenAI 上讨论的主要话题。”奥特曼还承诺在公司设立独立评估员，称这是一个“好主意”。
周日，Altman 表示 OpenAI 欢迎“为前沿人工智能设定一致安全要求的联邦框架”。他补充说，OpenAI 希望其他公司“学习我们的方法并提出自己的方法；我们认为针对偏差、监控和安全的共同标准将带来更好的结果。”与阿莫代一样，奥特曼也表示，“当我们谈论‘节奏’时，我们并不是指‘停止’，并指出进展应该‘比原本可能的速度慢’。”
奥特曼还指出，他认为人工智能进步“可能会非常糟糕”的两种方式：失去“人工智能对未来的控制”，最终“进入一个权力过于集中的世界”，他说，可以通过“走一条狭窄的中间道路”来避免这种情况。
谷歌 DeepMind 联合创始人兼主席 Demis Hassabis
“达里奥的文章指出了正确的前进道路，”哈萨比斯在回复阿莫迪的文章时说道。 “细节需要解决，但应对这个关键时刻的方向是正确的。”哈萨比斯还提到了他在 7 月份发布的人工智能标准机构框架。
SpaceX 首席执行官埃隆·马斯克
“达里奥是对的，”马斯克转发阿莫迪的文章说道。
美国总统唐纳德·特朗普
在周一早上的《真相社会》一篇漫无目的的帖子中，特朗普反驳了人工智能放缓的观点：

人工智能需要的唯一控制或“护栏”是一位坚强而聪明（高智商！）的总统，而美国确实拥有这样的总统！特朗普政府已经阻止人工智能“人”做坏事或可能做坏事的“事”，比如达里奥（人类！），他现在假装是一个“完美的小天使”——我们将继续这样做！我们已经对这些公司拥有巨大的刑事和监管权力！一场针对人工智能和数据中心的阴谋正在上演，唯一对此感到高兴的是中国。谁赢得了人工智能，谁就获胜了！我们正在引领中国和所有其他国家，并将继续这样做。阴谋论者、叛国者、叛徒和泄密者，请当心！感谢您对此事的关注！唐纳德·J·特朗普总统
英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋
在一次活动的台上，黄仁勋在一次活动的台上接听特朗普的电话，并把总统放在免提电话上，他说“机器人不会接管”，黄说，“我们将确保每个人都在美国的人工智能竞赛中获胜。每个行业、每个公司、每个州、每个人。”
美国副总统 JD 万斯
万斯表示，他觉得前沿人工智能科技公司“来到政府并恳求政府对其进行监管”，这“有点奇怪”，并补充说，“对我来说，这有点像特洛伊木马”。他还指出总统说：“我们知道中国正在与美国进行这场长期的人工智能竞赛。”
众议院议长迈克·约翰逊
作为周日接受 CNN 杰克·塔珀采访的一部分，约翰逊表示，“我认为所有这些平台的领导人和提供商......他们需要与我们开会，坐下来找出正确的平衡点。我们不能暂停这一计划，因为中国会与我们重叠。这就是挑战。这是国家安全与确保模型安全的直接安全之间的平衡。”目前尚不清楚这次会议是否或何时真正举行，但约翰逊表示他将“明天”举行。
参议员伯尼·桑德斯
桑德斯表示，他同意《华尔街日报》专栏作家、前罗纳德·里根演讲撰稿人佩吉·努南的观点，佩吉·努南发表了一篇题为“为了人类而暂停人工智能”的文章。
前交通部长皮特·布蒂吉格
布蒂吉格在接受美国全国广播公司新闻采访时表示：“国会袖手旁观，白宫无所作为，这对美国人民和世界来说都是非常危险的。” “需要有保障措施，需要有规则，需要有限制，需要有一个针对流氓人工智能的终止开关。”
前白宫人工智能和加密货币沙皇大卫·萨克斯
萨克斯在 X 上发表的一篇长文中表示：“达里奥曾写道，我们需要‘开拓前沿’，萨姆也同意了。”“人们可能会对我的回答感到惊讶：继续吧。”萨克斯还告诉他们“不要假装你需要其他人的许可”，“不要假装放慢速度的动机纯粹是无私的”。
前联邦贸易委员会主席莉娜·汗
“执法者已经有权对制造和发布危险的、未经审查的或有缺陷的产品的公司及其首席执行官提出指控，”汗在 X 上发表了一篇长篇文章时说道。“我们不应该让有关新法律制度的讨论分散人们对这样一个事实的注意力：现有的法律没有人工智能豁免权——@FTC 在我任职期间反复强调了这一点。”
前副总统卡马拉·哈里斯
哈里斯在帖子中表示：“我们必须负责任地放慢前沿人工智能的发展步伐，并补充说，为了确保人工智能服务于公众利益，放慢速度至关重要。”
前 Meta 首席人工智能科学家 Yann LeCun
“早在 2019 年，Dario 就已经声称 GPT2 太危险了，不能开源，”LeCun 在 X 上的回复中说道，“当时我取笑了他们。现在每个人都应该取笑他们。”

fulltext: Samsung Newsroom
Korea on September 14, 2026
Showcasing the industry’s first AI-powered ISAC trial on vRAN, the companies proved how sensing networks enable real-time intelligence for large-scale events

Samsung Electronics and Verizon have successfully completed an Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) trial at a major international soccer fan event in Dallas, Texas, enabling real-time sensing-driven intelligence across a virtualized network. This landmark milestone represents one of the industry’s first practical implementations of a key technology for 6G, signaling how operators are leveraging software-driven network architectures to create infrastructure that actively perceives, understands, and responds to their environment — moving beyond connectivity.

The groundbreaking field trial reinforces the value of the strategic partnership between Samsung and Verizon. Operating one of the world’s largest commercial virtualized networks, Verizon has led the charge in deploying a software-driven, AI-powered virtualized RAN (vRAN). This laid the foundation for a 6G-ready platform necessary to bring experimental use cases from concept to real-world validation — highlighting the flexibility of Samsung’s adaptable vRAN, which enables operators to introduce new capabilities like ISAC from day one by leveraging the commercial network they already run.

In the ISAC trial, Samsung integrated commercial AI-powered vRAN and vCore with an ISAC application, deploying them on its Network in a Server (NIS) — an end-to-end software-driven edge-AI platform that consolidates all network functions and accelerated compute into a single server. This allowed the ISAC trial to leverage connectivity from a 5G network without the need for any additional equipment.

Acting as a sensing receiver, a CBRS1 radio unit using 40 MHz of spectrum mounted on a Verizon Cell-On-Wheels (COW) captured channel variations in transmissions from a commercial 5G device. Samsung’s NIS then analyzed this real-time data, utilizing the accelerated compute to extract actionable insights that are visualized as a crowd density heatmap that changes in near-real time to reflect people’s movements.2

Operating live at the event, the ISAC system used wireless signals as a sensing basis to automatically identify crowded areas within the venue, proving how sensing capabilities can enhance event management and the visitor experience across multiple stakeholder groups:

The achievement reflects the synergy between Samsung’s commercial technologies and its advanced research in accelerating the path to 6G. The company’s efforts include its commercially proven vRAN software on the edge-AI platform NIS, and Samsung Research America’s (SRA) cutting-edge AI-driven ISAC solution.

“Verizon’s strategy has always been focused on building an intelligent, AI-native network that translates into meaningful real-world value for our customers,” said Yago Tenorio, Chief Technology Officer and Senior Vice President of Technology Development at Verizon. “Our early investments in flexible, software-driven vRAN architecture are paying off today, giving us the agility to engineer and trial groundbreaking 6G concepts like ISAC over our existing infrastructure. This field trial with Samsung proves that the network of the future will do far more than just transfer data — it will actively perceive and interact with its environment to transform venue management and public safety.”

“This successful ISAC trial underscores how Verizon’s decision to adopt a software-driven, AI-powered vRAN early on laid a solid foundation, positioning the company at the forefront of the 6G journey,” said Ji-Yun Seol, Executive Vice President and Head of Product Strategy, Networks Business at Samsung Electronics. “With this approach, forward-thinking operators like Verizon are unlocking untapped potential, spearheading the shift toward a new era where unprecedented services, devices, and use cases converge on next-generation networks.”

“This ISAC trial marks a significant leap forward in integrating AI-driven sensing capabilities into network infrastructure, showcasing the transformative potential of 6G technologies,” said Charlie Zhang, Executive Vice President at Samsung Research America. “By combining Verizon’s innovative approach with Samsung’s advanced vRAN solutions, we’ve demonstrated the practical application of ISAC in a real-world scenario to enhance safety, efficiency, and user experience. This collaboration reinforces our commitment to pushing the boundaries of what’s possible in next-generation wireless networks.”

As a founding member of the Verizon 6G Innovation Forum, Samsung is exploring new use cases to advance innovation, research initiatives, and the overall charter of the consortium. The company continues to work alongside visionary partners to deliver transformative technologies and drive the transition to 6G.

Samsung Networks has pioneered the successful delivery of 5G end-to-end solutions, including chipsets, radios, and cores. Through ongoing research and development, Samsung is driving the industry to advance 5G networks and paving the way for 6G and beyond with its market-leading product portfolio, from purpose-built RAN, vRAN, Open RAN, AI RAN, and cloud-native core to private network solutions and AI-powered automation tools (CognitiV NOS). The company currently provides innovative network solutions to mobile operators that deliver boundless connectivity to hundreds of millions of users worldwide.

两家公司展示了业界首个基于人工智能的 vRAN ISAC 试验，证明了传感网络如何为大型事件提供实时情报
三星电子和 Verizon 在德克萨斯州达拉斯举行的一次大型国际足球迷活动中成功完成了集成传感和通信 (ISAC) 试验，从而在虚拟化网络中实现实时传感驱动的智能。这一具有里程碑意义的里程碑代表了业界首批 6G 关键技术的实际实施之一，标志着运营商如何利用软件驱动的网络架构来创建主动感知、理解和响应环境的基础设施——超越连接性。

此次突破性的现场试验强化了三星与 Verizon 之间战略合作伙伴关系的价值。 Verizon 运营着全球最大的商业虚拟化网络之一，在部署软件驱动、人工智能驱动的虚拟化 RAN (vRAN) 方面处于领先地位。这为将实验用例从概念带入现实世界验证所必需的 6G 就绪平台奠定了基础，凸显了三星适应性强的 vRAN 的灵活性，使运营商能够从第一天起就利用他们已经运行的商业网络引入 ISAC 等新功能。
在 ISAC 试验中，三星将商用 AI 驱动的 vRAN 和 vCore 与 ISAC 应用程序集成，并将其部署在服务器网络 (NIS) 上，NIS 是一个端到端软件驱动的边缘 AI 平台，可将所有网络功能和加速计算整合到单个服务器中。这使得 ISAC 试验能够利用 5G 网络的连接，而无需任何额外的设备。
安装在 Verizon Cell-On-Wheels (COW) 上的 CBRS1 无线电单元使用 40 MHz 频谱，充当传感接收器，捕获商用 5G 设备传输中的信道变化。然后，三星的 NIS 分析了这些实时数据，利用加速计算来提取可操作的见解，这些见解被可视化为人群密度热图，该图近乎实时地变化以反映人们的活动。2
ISAC 系统在活动现场运行，使用无线信号作为传感基础，自动识别场馆内的拥挤区域，证明传感功能如何能够增强活动管理和多个利益相关群体的访客体验：
这一成就反映了三星商业技术与其先进研究在加速 6G 道路上的协同作用。该公司的努力包括在边缘人工智能平台 NIS 上提供经过商业验证的 vRAN 软件，以及三星美国研究院 (SRA) 的尖端人工智能驱动的 ISAC 解决方案。

Verizon 首席技术官兼技术开发高级副总裁 Yago Tenorio 表示：“Verizon 的战略始终专注于构建智能、人工智能原生网络，为我们的客户转化为有意义的现实价值。” “我们对灵活、软件驱动的 vRAN 架构的早期投资如今已获得回报，使我们能够在现有基础设施上灵活地设计和试验 ISAC 等突破性 6G 概念。与三星的此次现场试验证明，未来的网络将不仅仅只是传输数据，还将主动感知环境并与其交互，从而改变场馆管理和公共安全。”
三星电子网络业务执行副总裁兼产品战略主管 Ji-Yun Seol 表示：“ISAC 试验的成功凸显了 Verizon 在早期就采用软件驱动、人工智能驱动的 vRAN 的决定奠定了坚实的基础，使该公司处于 6G 征程的最前沿。” “通过这种方法，像 Verizon 这样具有前瞻性思维的运营商正在释放未开发的潜力，引领向新时代的转变，前所未有的服务、设备和用例将汇聚到下一代网络上。”
三星美国研究院执行副总裁张查理表示：“此次 ISAC 试验标志着将人工智能驱动的传感功能集成到网络基础设施方面的重大飞跃，展示了 6G 技术的变革潜力。” “通过将 Verizon 的创新方法与三星先进的 vRAN 解决方案相结合，我们展示了 ISAC 在现实场景中的实际应用，以提高安全性、效率和用户体验。此次合作强化了我们对突破下一代无线网络可能性界限的承诺。”
作为 Verizon 6G 创新论坛的创始成员，三星正在探索新的用例，以推进创新、研究计划和联盟的整体章程。该公司继续与有远见的合作伙伴合作，提供变革性技术并推动向 6G 的过渡。
三星网络率先成功交付 5G 端到端解决方案，包括芯片组、无线电和核心。通过持续的研发，三星正在推动行业推进 5G 网络，并凭借其市场领先的产品组合为 6G 及更高版本铺平道路，从专用 RAN、vRAN、Open RAN、AI RAN 和云原生核心到专用网络解决方案和人工智能驱动的自动化工具 (CognitiV NOS)。该公司目前为移动运营商提供创新的网络解决方案，为全球数亿用户提供无限的连接。

While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was onstage at the All-In Summit on Monday morning in Los Angeles, he got a phone call that he couldn’t send to voicemail — it was from President Donald Trump.

“I’m onstage with the besties,” Huang told Trump, referring to the venture capitalists who host the podcast All-In, including tech investors Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, and White House advisers David Friedberg and David Sacks.
In a move that will spark night terrors for public relations professionals everywhere, Huang flaunted his comfort with the president by putting Trump on speaker for conference attendees to hear.

Holy crap POTUS just phoned in @JensenHuang live on stage at All In SummitWe will not lose the ai race! And whatever Dario said this weekend won’t stop our progressThis made my morning!$NVDA pic.twitter.com/Sr4wV9kMfz

“The great thing about life is Jensen can develop the most complex computer chip in the world… but he can’t figure out how to put you on speaker,” Trump said on the phone. (Huang is likely aware of how speakerphones work; he was asking stagehands for an extra microphone so that he could project the call to the audience.)

Onstage, Huang and the All-In hosts had been discussing Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI.” SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have publicly said they agree with Amodei, while Huang’s views have diverged.

“They’re just playing right in the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen,” Trump said. “That could be political people. It could also be China. And we’re not going to let that happen. It’s a hoax.”
“You’re right. We’re not going to let that happen, sir,” Huang replied as the crowd broke into applause.

Trump and his allies, like Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, have stated their belief that the growing sentiment against data center construction is part of an international psyop to stifle American economic growth. But the source of the public’s concern is more straightforward. Recent Gallup polling shows that seven in 10 Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their area, with more than 50% of respondents citing the effect of data centers on environmental resources. About 20% said they were concerned about cost-of-living increases and effects on their quality of life.

“We have to be a little bit careful… We have to do things and we have to do them prudently, but that doesn’t mean we’re going to stop an industry,” Trump said to Huang. “So I’m with you all the way. I didn’t even know how you felt about it. I just hoped you felt the same way as me. We’re going to lead.”

“我和我的好朋友们一起在台上，”黄告诉特朗普，他指的是主持播客 All-In 的风险投资家，包括科技投资者查马斯·帕里哈皮蒂亚 (Chamath Palihapitiya)、杰森·卡拉卡尼斯 (Jason Calacanis) 以及白宫顾问大卫·弗里德伯格 (David Friedberg) 和大卫·萨克斯 (David Sacks)。
此举将引发世界各地公关专业人士的夜惊，黄把特朗普放在扬声器上供与会者聆听，以此炫耀他对总统的安慰。
天哪，美国总统刚刚在 All In Summit 的舞台上现场给 @JensenHuang 打电话，我们不会输掉人工智能竞赛！不管达里奥这个周末说什么都不会阻止我们的进步这让我早上很开心！$NVDA pic.twitter.com/Sr4wV9kMfz
“生活中最伟大的事情是詹森可以开发出世界上最复杂的计算机芯片......但他不知道如何让你打开扬声器，”特朗普在电话中说。 （黄很可能知道免提电话的工作原理；他向舞台工作人员索要一个额外的麦克风，以便他可以将通话投射给观众。）
在台上，黄仁勋和 All-In 主持人一直在讨论 Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 的呼吁，即“放慢我们提高人工智能能力的步伐”。 SpaceX 首席执行官埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 和 OpenAI 首席执行官萨姆·奥尔特曼 (Sam Altman) 曾公开表示他们同意 Amodei 的观点，而黄仁勋的观点则存在分歧。
特朗普说：“他们只是在很多不希望看到这种情况发生的人手中发挥作用。” “这可能是政治人物。也可能是中国。我们不会让这种情况发生。这是一个骗局。”
“您是对的。我们不会让这种事发生，先生。”黄回答道，人群爆发出热烈的掌声。
特朗普和 Y Combinator 首席执行官加里·谭 (Garry Tan) 等盟友表示，他们相信，反对数据中心建设的情绪日益高涨，是扼杀美国经济增长的国际心理战的一部分。但公众担忧的根源更为直接。最近的盖洛普民意调查显示，十分之七的美国人反对在其所在地区建设数据中心，超过 50% 的受访者指出数据中心对环境资源的影响。大约 20% 的人表示，他们担心生活成本的增加及其对生活质量的影响。
“我们必须小心一点……我们必须做事，我们必须谨慎行事，但这并不意味着我们要停止一个行业，”特朗普对黄说。 “所以我一直和你在一起。我什至不知道你对此有何感受。我只是希望你和我有同样的感受。我们将领先。”
